The utilization rates of intraductal ultrasonography (IDUS) and cholangioscopy were not significantly different across the cohorts, with p -values of 0.384 and 0.762, respectively. The prevalence of a history of digestive tract reconstruction and diabetes mellitus was also comparable among the groups, with p -values of 0.811 and 0.136, respectively. Outcome assessment and definitions PEC was defined as the onset of a new fever (body temperature >38 °C) accompanied by an elevated white blood cell count, increased C-reactive protein levels, and worsening liver function tests, persisting for more than 24 h after ERCP ( , ). Cases involving pulmonary infection, acute pancreatitis, and other unrelated infections were excluded. Cholangitis was classified as mild, moderate, or severe according to the Tokyo Guidelines ( ). Mild cases were managed with antibiotics alone, while moderate cases required early biliary reintervention, such as endoscopic or percutaneous drainage. All severity grades were included in the study. Statistical analysis shows that the majority of the cases were mild, and antibiotic treatment was effective. However, we observed that some patients with biliary strictures required prolonged antibiotic treatment after ERCP, frequently guided by bile or blood culture results. These individuals showed a higher propensity for infections with resistant bacteria, such as Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium , necessitating the use of broader-spectrum or more advanced antibiotics ( ). The grading of inflammation severity in PEC patients, the duration of antibiotic use, and the results of bacterial culture were shown in . Predictive model The candidate predictors, Sex, Age, Wbc, Hb, Alt, Tbil, GGT, Alb, CEA, CA19-9, etiology, gallstone, digestive tract reconstruction, stenosis site, diabetes, obstruction length, ERCP operation time, EST, EPBD, ENBD, ERBD, Cytology Brush, EMBE, Spyglass, operators, and IDUS, were included in the original model, which was then reduced to 8 potential predictors using LASSO regression analysis performed in the training cohort. A cross-validated error plot of the LASSO regression model is shown in . The most regularized and parsimonious model, with a cross-validated error within one standard error of the minimum, included 8 variables. The details of the selected features are shown in . As shown in , the ROC analysis of the abovementioned variables yielded AUC values greater than 0.5. Further multivariate logistic analyses were carried out in different cohorts. Results are shown in . The final logistic model included 8 independent predictors Age, Alb, Digestive tract reconstruction, Stenosis site, Diabetes, ERCP operation time (h), obstruction length and Cholangioscopy was developed as a simple-to-use nomogram, which is illustrated in . Validation of the model The figures below display the AUCs of the model in different cohorts. The pooled area under the ROC curve of the nomogram for the predictive model was 0.760 in the training set and 0.787 in the validation set, indicating strong performance ( ). Calibration plots of the nomogram in various cohorts show a positive correlation between observed and predicted cholangitis ( ). These results confirm that the original nomogram remains valid for use in validation sets, with its calibration curve closely resembling the ideal curve and demonstrating consistent predicted results with actual findings. Decision curve analysis displays the DCA curves related to the nomogram. This research shows that the nomogram offers substantial net benefits for clinical application through its DCA curve. The Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) demonstrated that our model provides a positive net benefit across a wide range of threshold probabilities. Considering the high baseline risk of PEC in biliary stricture patients and the severity of potential outcomes, a threshold probability range of 10 to 40% is deemed clinically reasonable for initiating prophylactic antibiotics. Within this range, our model outperformed both the “treat-all” and “treat-none” strategies, offering a superior balance between sensitivity and specificity. Discussion Biliary stricture can be divided into benign stenosis and malignant stenosis. The causes of benign stenosis include bile duct inflammation, bile duct stones, and iatrogenic bile duct injury, etc. The causes of malignant stenosis include liver cancer, bile duct cancer, pancreatic cancer, and so on ( , , ). Patients with biliary strictures are more likely to develop cholangitis ( , ). Patients with biliary stricture often require ERCP procedures for diagnosis and treatment ( , , ). ERCP is an invasive operation, and due to the complex structure of duodenoscopes, leads to more complications, such as PEC ( , ). The occurring incidence ranges from 1% to 5% ( ). PEC incidence can reach up to 20% in patients with biliary stricture ( ). PEC can delay the length of hospital stay, increase the economic burden of patients, and even threaten the life of patients. If we can assess the risk of PEC in patients with biliary stricture early, we can treat it as early as possible and avoid the progression of the disease. In the current study, we developed and validated a nomogram for predicting PEC, based on a cohort of biliary stricture patients. The main predictors incorporated into the nomogram included Age, Alb, digestive tract reconstruction, etiology, stenosis site, diabetes, obstruction length, ERCP operation time and the use of cholangioscopy, which were statistically significant in multivariate logistic regression analysis. To our knowledge, this is the first study to predict the risk of cholangitis after ERCP in patients with biliary strictures. ESGE suggested that hilar obstruction, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and cholangioscopy were the high-risk factors for PEC ( ). In a recent retrospective study, age over 60 years and the history of ERCP is an independent risk factor for PEC ( ). Whereas previous studies have focused on non-selective populations, our study was performed on patients diagnosed with specific biliary strictures. Our study was more specific and focused on patients with biliary stricture to evaluate the situation of cholangitis after ERCP. Variables examined in the study includes the basic characteristics of the patients, the characteristics of stenosis, and ERCP-related operations. We found that Age, Alb, digestive tract reconstruction, stenosis site, diabetes, obstruction length, ERCP operation time (h), and the use of cholangioscopy were the risk factors for PEC in biliary strictures. We combined these variables to establish and validate a novel predictive tool for PEC for patients with biliary strictures. The nomogram of this study provides several clinical significances. First, it provides clinicians with a quantitative tool that can predict the risk of PEC more accurately than traditional methods, contributing to better risk stratification. In addition, early identification of high-risk individuals by this nomogram could lead to timely interventions and potentially reduce morbidity and mortality. There are some risk factors that we cannot change. For example, the Location of Stricture and the Length of the Stricture cannot be changed. Some factors, such as good control of the blood glucose and elevated level of Alb can reduce the occurrence of PEC. Who should receive antibiotic prophylaxis before ERCP remains controversial ( ). Some believed that prophylactic antibiotics are not necessary for all patients before ERCP and may have little effect on the prevention of cholangitis, but may reduce the risk of bacteremia ( , ). The ESGE guidelines state that preoperative prophylactic antibiotics can be used in patients with expected inadequate biliary drainage, and severe immune insufficiency, and when choledochoscopy is performed ( ). We suggest that the PEC high-risk patients with bile duct stricture undergo preoperative use of antibiotics to prevent infection. The clinically relevant threshold for initiating prophylaxis in this group is shifted upwards (estimated 5%–25%). Our DCA demonstrates that even within this high-risk context, a “treat-all” strategy is not optimal, particularly when the acceptable risk threshold exceeds 18%. Our model provides superior net benefit in this range, supporting a precision medicine approach to antibiotic prophylaxis even among high-risk subgroups. Patients with hilar biliary strictures as well as intrahepatic strictures have a higher risk of developing PEC than patients with extrahepatic strictures. PSC, ICC, h-CCA, and metastatic tumors are the main causes of hilar strictures and intrahepatic strictures. These patients have long, multi-vessel biliary strictures and are in poor physical condition, requiring multiple stents for drainage. Although the use of choledochoscopy may increase the risk of PEC, choledochoscopy is of great value in the differential diagnosis of benign and malignant biliary strictures ( ). SpyGlass-guided visual impression combined with SpyBite was better for differential diagnosis of benign and malignant bile duct strictures in terms of sensitivity and accuracy compared with conventional endoscopic diagnostic methods such as cytobrush ( , ). Furthermore, Spyglass can assist the operator in performing selective cannulaiton in cases where the bile duct is severely narrowed ( ). Literature and guidelines mention the

are in poor physical condition, requiring multiple stents for drainage. Although the use of choledochoscopy may increase the risk of PEC, choledochoscopy is of great value in the differential diagnosis of benign and malignant biliary strictures ( ). SpyGlass-guided visual impression combined with SpyBite was better for differential diagnosis of benign and malignant bile duct strictures in terms of sensitivity and accuracy compared with conventional endoscopic diagnostic methods such as cytobrush ( , ). Furthermore, Spyglass can assist the operator in performing selective cannulaiton in cases where the bile duct is severely narrowed ( ). Literature and guidelines mention the use of antibiotics in patients undergoing choledochoscopy, especially elderly patients and those with prior stent placement or intraduct lithotripsy ( ). Othman et al. ( ) reported that the use of choledochoscopy may be associated with an 8.8% incidence of bacteremia and a 7% incidence of cholangitis. In our study, it was found that the probability of PEC caused by choledochoscopy in patients with biliary stricture was even more than 20%. This might be due to the fact that in our research cohort, there were a greater number of cases of hilar bile duct stenosis, and the proportion of difficult ERCP procedures was also higher. Using antibiotics before the surgery and reducing the amount of fluid injected during the operation may be effective methods to reduce the infection rate caused by choledochoscopy ( ). However, more research data is needed to support the viewpoint. Although our study does not suggest the predictive value of EST and EPBD, it does not mean that these procedures have no effect. In our study, minor EST (3–5 mm)with or without small EPBD (6–8 mm) was used to avoid the destruction of the papillary sphincter and reduce the risk of retrograde infection. In addition, we found that digestive tract reconstruction increases the risk of PEC. Common digestive tract reconstruction surgery includes subtotal gastrectomy, bilioenteric anastomosis, pancreaticoduodenectomy, and so on ( ). These operations not only increase the difficulty of endoscopic intervention but also are associated with a high incidence of postoperative complications. Some patients may require Endoscopic Ultrasound-Guided Biliary Drainage (EUS-BD) due to the failure of conventional ERCP. However, the relationship between EUS-BD and PEC warrants further investigation. Although our study has achieved some success, it also has some limitations. In this model, operator experience may vary across hospitals. If the operator is inexperienced, this may further increase the risk of PEC in patients with biliary strictures. Future research should aim to externally validate our nomogram in diverse populations and settings. Additionally, integrating novel predictors or biomarkers can enhance the predictive accuracy of the nomogram, which deserves further investigation. Limitations Our Decision Curve Analysis focused specifically on the prevention of Post-ERCP Cholangitis (PEC) as the primary outcome. While this reflects the critical importance of preventing sepsis in patients with biliary strictures, we did not explicitly incorporate competing harms from other potential complications (e.g., post-ERCP pancreatitis, pneumonia) or specific antibiotic-related adverse events into the net benefit calculation. Consequently, the estimated net benefit primarily applies to clinical scenarios where preventing PEC is the dominant decision driver. Future studies incorporating a multi-outcome framework could provide a more holistic assessment of clinical utility.

documents.title: ESGE Guideline Diagnosis and Management of Nonvariceal Upper GI Hemorrhage

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage (UGIB), originating from anatomical sites superior to the ligament of Treitz, is a significant contributor to morbidity and mortality worldwide. [ ] Despite advances in endoscopic interventions and pharmacologic therapy, the mortality rate associated with UGIB remains approximately 5-10%, with no discernible change over the past two decades. [ ] The primary causes include peptic ulcer disease, erosive gastroduodenal mucosal lesions, Mallory-Weiss syndrome, and neoplastic conditions of the upper gastrointestinal tract. [ ] Endoscopic therapy is the first-line treatment for UGIB. Bleeding can be managed with an 85-95% success rate using endoscopic methods. [ ] However, endoscopic management may fail in cases of massive bleeding, anatomically inaccessible lesions, or refractory bleeding despite initial hemostasis. In the past, surgery was considered the standard salvage therapy for failures of endoscopic procedures. However, surgical management is associated with significant morbidity rates ranging from 20% to 40% and mortality rates between 10% and 30%, especially in elderly patients with comorbidities. [ , ] Transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) has emerged as an alternative to surgery for patients with refractory UGIB. Advances in microcatheter technology, embolic agents, and imaging guidance have improved TAE's technical success and safety profile. [ , ] Despite the increasing adoption of TAE for UGIB, there remains debate regarding its efficacy compared to surgical intervention, particularly concerning rebleeding rates, long-term outcomes, and specific patient populations who might benefit most from each approach. [ ] This study aimed to assess the technical success, clinical effectiveness, and safety profile of empiric TAE for UGIB and to compare these outcomes with those reported for surgical interventions in the current literature. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study Design and Patient Selection This study was designed as a single-center, retrospective analysis. Ethics committee approval was granted for the study (16.01.2025/E-43012747-050.04-438245). Because of its retrospective design, the study was exempt from the requirement for informed consent. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. We reviewed the electronic medical records of 33 consecutive patients referred to interventional radiology for embolization due to UGIB between August 2021 and November 2024. All patients included in the study were first evaluated with endoscopy. TAE was performed in patients whose bleeding could not be controlled by endoscopic interventions. The files of 33 patients referred to the interventional radiology department by the general surgery service for upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding were analyzed. Eight patients who were unsuitable for TAE and five who did not consent to TAE were excluded from the study. Twenty patients (6 males, 14 females) with a mean age of 62.3 years (range: 19-84 years) were included in the study ( ). Inclusion criteria were: (1) patients with endoscopically confirmed or clinically suspected UGIB; (2) failure of or contraindication to endoscopic management; (3) referral for interventional radiological management; and (4) patients who gave consent to endovascular treatment. Exclusion criteria were: (1) lower gastrointestinal bleeding; (2) incomplete medical records; (3) patients who underwent prophylactic embolization before elective surgery; and (4) patients who did not give consent to endovascular treatment. Data Collection Patient demographic data, clinical parameters, procedural details, and outcomes were collected from electronic medical records. The following parameters were recorded: age, sex, pre- and post-procedure hemoglobin levels, indication for embolization, target vessel, embolic agent, technical success, clinical success, complications, and endoscopic findings. Embolization Procedure All interventions were conducted by experienced interventional radiologists in a specialized angiography suite. Following the administration of local anesthesia, access to the femoral artery was achieved using a 5F femoral sheath (Shunmei, China). An initial abdominal aortography was performed by selective catheterization of the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery using a 5-French diagnostic catheter (Performa, Merit Medical, Ireland). Thereafter, super-selective catheterization of the gastroduodenal artery (GDA) or left gastric artery (LGA) was carried out using a microcatheter system (Progreat, Terumo, Japan). Embolization was performed once the bleeding site was identified or prophylactically based on endoscopic findings. Embolic materials included microcoils (Interlock, Boston Scientific, USA) for the GDA and particles (Embosphere, Merit Medical, Ireland) for the LGA. Clinical success was defined as target-area devascularization resulting in clinical cessation of bleeding and stabilization of hemoglobin levels. Technical success was defined as occlusion of the feeding vessel and/or absence of extravasation following angiography. Outcome Measures The primary outcome measures included the rate of technical success (successful placement of embolic agents in the intended vessel) and clinical success (cessation of bleeding without signs of rebleeding within 30 days). Secondary outcome measures encompassed changes in hemoglobin levels, complication rates, duration of hospitalization, and mortality rates within 30 days. The reporting guidelines established by the Society of Interventional Radiology classified complications as either minor or major. Minor complications were defined as those requiring only observation without intervention or hospitalization. In contrast, major complications were those necessitating prolonged hospitalization, an unplanned increase in the level of patient

Outcome Measures The primary outcome measures included the rate of technical success (successful placement of embolic agents in the intended vessel) and clinical success (cessation of bleeding without signs of rebleeding within 30 days). Secondary outcome measures encompassed changes in hemoglobin levels, complication rates, duration of hospitalization, and mortality rates within 30 days. The reporting guidelines established by the Society of Interventional Radiology classified complications as either minor or major. Minor complications were defined as those requiring only observation without intervention or hospitalization. In contrast, major complications were those necessitating prolonged hospitalization, an unplanned increase in the level of patient care, or resulting in sequelae or death. Rebleeding was defined as hematemesis, melena, or a decrease in hemoglobin concentration of ≥2 g/dL following initial stabilization. [ ] Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were employed to describe patient demographics and clinical outcomes. Continuous variables were tested for normality using the Shapiro–Wilk test. As the data did not follow a normal distribution, pre- and post-procedure hemoglobin levels were compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired samples. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Continuous variables were presented as mean±standard deviation, depending on distribution. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages. All analyses were performed using SPSS version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). RESULTS The most common indications for embolization were duodenal ulcers (n=5, 25%), gastric malignancies (n=5, 25%), and gastric ulcers (n=4, 20%). Other indications included esophageal varices with gastric ulcer (n=1, 5%), post-surgical anastomotic bleeding (n=1, 5%), and undocumented indications (n=4, 20%). summarizes the baseline characteristics of the study population. Technical Outcomes Of the 20 patients who underwent embolization, 13 (65%) had duodenal bleeding, for which gastroduodenal artery embolization was performed. The remaining seven patients (35%) had gastric bleeding and were treated with left gastric artery embolization. The procedure was successful in all patients (100%), achieving both technical and clinical success. Coils were exclusively used in patients with duodenal bleeding (n=13, 65%), while particles were the embolic agents of choice in all gastric artery embolization cases (n=7, 35%). This approach was tailored to the specific site of bleeding and the vascular anatomy of the patients ( ). Rebleeding was observed in one patient (5%) and was managed surgically. A major complication, coil migration, was noted in one patient (5%) and was resolved with conservative management. Additionally, one patient (5%) experienced a minor complication, a groin hematoma, which did not require transfusion. No procedure-related deaths occurred. Clinical Outcomes Before the procedure, the average hemoglobin level was 7.9±1.9 g/dL, increasing to 8.3±1.2 g/dL post-procedure, representing a mean increase of 0.4 g/dL (p=0.15). Clinical success, defined as cessation of bleeding without rebleeding within 30 days, was achieved in 19 of the 20 patients (95%), although follow-up data were limited for some patients. Complications occurred in two patients (10%), including coil migration in one patient (5%) and a groin hematoma in another (5%). These complications did not necessitate further interventions or result in clinical deterioration. No procedure-related deaths were recorded. Endoscopic evaluation after the procedure was performed in 12 patients (60%) and demonstrated resolution of active bleeding in all cases, although some patients had persistent ulcers or malignant lesions. DISCUSSION This retrospective analysis demonstrates that TAE is an effective and safe treatment for UGIB, showing excellent technical and clinical success rates and a manageable complication profile. A unique aspect of our study is the inclusion of gastroduodenal artery and left gastric artery treatments, as well as the use of both coils and microspheres. Our findings are consistent with previous studies reporting technical success rates ranging from 82% to 100% and clinical success rates from 65% to 93% for TAE in UGIB cases. [ , ] Our technical success rate of 100% is comparable to other published series. The single technical failure occurred due to instability of a coil in the gastroduodenal artery stump, highlighting the importance of careful coil selection and deployment techniques. Alternative embolic agents, such as gelatin sponge particles or liquid embolic agents, may be employed when coil deployment is challenging. [ ] The clinical success rate of 100% is at the higher end of the range reported in the literature. This may reflect appropriate patient selection, technical expertise, and the use of suitable embolic agents based on bleeding characteristics. The choice of embolic agent remains somewhat controversial, with microcoils preferred for their precision and permanence. At the same time, particles allow more distal embolization but carry a theoretical risk of ischemic complications. [ ] Regarding safety, our complication rate of 15% is consistent with published rates of 9-20%. [ ] The observed complications were related to coil placement and were managed conservatively without clinical sequelae. Our series did not observe major complications such as bowel ischemia, which has been reported in 0-5% of cases in the literature. This may

the use of suitable embolic agents based on bleeding characteristics. The choice of embolic agent remains somewhat controversial, with microcoils preferred for their precision and permanence. At the same time, particles allow more distal embolization but carry a theoretical risk of ischemic complications. [ ] Regarding safety, our complication rate of 15% is consistent with published rates of 9-20%. [ ] The observed complications were related to coil placement and were managed conservatively without clinical sequelae. Our series did not observe major complications such as bowel ischemia, which has been reported in 0-5% of cases in the literature. This may be attributed to careful technique with super-selective catheterization and embolization, preserving collateral circulation. [ ] When comparing TAE with surgery for UGIB, our results suggest that TAE is similarly effective but carries a better safety profile, particularly for high-risk patients. Surgical interventions may have slightly higher technical success rates but are associated with increased morbidity (30-50%) and mortality (5-15%). [ - ] The less invasive nature of TAE makes it an ideal option for elderly patients or those with significant comorbidities who may not be suitable candidates for major surgery. Numerous studies have sought to identify variables that predict the efficacy or inefficacy of TAE in treating UGIB. Factors such as coagulopathy, multiple comorbid conditions, hemodynamic instability, and corticosteroid use have been associated with increased rebleeding rates after TAE. [ ] Appropriate patient selection is paramount, with some authors advocating surgical intervention as the primary treatment modality for young, healthy individuals with significant hemorrhage, while recommending TAE for older patients or those with substantial comorbidities. [ - ] The anatomical location of bleeding may also influence the success of TAE. Gastroduodenal and left gastric artery embolization have shown higher success rates than embolization of other vessels, likely due to the rich collateral circulation in these regions. [ ] In our series, most embolizations involved the gastroduodenal artery, which may have contributed to the favorable outcomes. Recent innovations in embolization methodologies have further enhanced TAE's effectiveness and safety profile. The use of advanced microcatheters, detachable coils, and liquid embolic agents has improved procedural accuracy. Furthermore, the incorporation of cone-beam computed tomography within the angiography suite facilitates improved visualization of subtle hemorrhage and allows for more precise catheter placement. [ ] In addition to methodology, patient selection, pre-procedural evaluation, and post-procedural care are critical to effectiveness and safety. [ ] The minimally invasive approach offers clear benefits, particularly for high-risk patients with comorbidities, compared to the significant physiological stress imposed by traditional surgery. However, it is important to acknowledge the vital role of surgical intervention in the management of upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Surgery continues to be an essential treatment option due to its ability to achieve complete and lasting bleeding control through direct intervention at the hemorrhage site, particularly when transcatheter arterial embolization cannot be performed because of anatomical constraints or has failed to achieve the desired outcome. The successful surgical management of the 5% rebleeding rate observed in our study confirms that these two disciplines are not alternatives but complementary. Modern hemorrhage management should adopt a hybrid, patient-tailored approach, recognizing the strengths of both methods and fostering close collaboration between interventional radiology and surgery to achieve optimal patient outcomes. [ , ] Nevertheless, our study has several limitations. First, its retrospective nature introduces potential selection and information biases. Second, the relatively modest sample size limits statistical power and the ability to extrapolate our findings. Thirdly, follow-up data were not systematically collected for all patients, which may have resulted in underreporting of rebleeding incidences. Fourthly, our comparative analysis of surgical outcomes relied on published literature rather than direct comparisons, which may introduce confounding factors. Finally, the absence of consistent long-term follow-up beyond 30 days precludes the evaluation of late rebleeding or other delayed complications. CONCLUSION Transcatheter arterial embolization represents an effective and safe therapeutic modality for patients presenting with upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, characterized by high technical and clinical success rates and a manageable complication profile. Our findings support the use of TAE as a primary intervention for patients with UGIB who do not respond to endoscopic management, particularly those at high surgical risk.

chunks.content: Introduction Endoscopic therapy is integral to the management of Barrett’s-related neoplasia; low-grade dysplasia (LGD), high-grade dysplasia (HGD), and early EAC. Successful treatment relies on accurate optical diagnosis, complete removal of visible neoplasia, and ablation of residual Barrett’s mucosa to reduce metachronous disease [ ]. Outcomes are closely linked to expertise and centralised care, with higher detection rates, better histopathological accuracy, and improved long-term remission consistently demonstrated in specialist units. This review provides a structured overview of ER and ablation techniques, practical aspects of patient selection and follow-up, current evidence guiding therapeutic decisions and future directions in the field. Endoscopic Therapy – Overall Strategy The goal of endoscopic therapy in BE is to prevent morbidity and mortality secondary to EAC. In non-dysplastic BE, the rate of progression to EAC is low (0.3% per annum), and therefore surveillance over endoscopic treatment is favoured [ , ]. Where dysplasia or early (T1) EAC is detected, endoscopic eradication therapy (EET) is recommended, to reduce the risk of progression to advanced EAC [ ] through eradication of visible BE (CE-BE) and sustained long-term remission of BE-neoplasia. High-quality endoscopic therapy of BE hinges upon a coordinated, multidisciplinary, protocol-driven approach. Centralisation of care is key to achieving this aim. In their 2023 guideline, the European Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ESGE) recommend that patients with confirmed dysplasia or early cancer should be referred to a BE expert centre for further management [ ]. The criteria for defining an expert centre included the annual case volume per BE endoscopist, additional subspeciality training of both endoscopists and pathologists, a pathway for MDT discussion of all cases of BE dysplasia and cancer including experienced esophageal surgeons. The impact of expertise and case volume on neoplasia detection rates, accuracy of histopathological diagnosis and staging as well as technical and clinical success following endoscopic therapy has been repeatedly demonstrated [ – ]. The cornerstone of BE management is optical evaluation, as this informs all subsequent therapeutic decisions [ ]. Optimal BE assessment starts before the patient enters the endoscopy room; it begins with the appropriate assignment of cases to dedicated lists with sufficient time allocated, performed by a trained endoscopist in a suitably equipped unit using the latest high-definition endoscopes with virtual chromoendoscopy (VCE) capability. The ESGE outline recommendations for training in optical assessment for early BE-neoplasia, including the use of a validated online training module – Barrett’s Oesophagus-Related Neoplasia (BORN) for detection and delineation of lesions using white light endoscopy, as well as training in lesion characterisation using VCE and acetic acid [ , ]. A meticulous technique is required: the mucosa should first be thoroughly cleaned using water mixed with a mucosal cleansing agent, ensuring aspiration of all bubbles and residual fluid. This is followed by slow, considered inspection (≥1 min per centimetre of circumferential Barrett’s epithelium) and systematic lesion characterisation using the Paris Classification and VCE to assess surface features [ ]. Endoscopic eradication of BE is the recommended standard of care for BE dysplasia and early EAC due to its excellent safety and long-term efficacy [ , ]. This comprises a “two-step” concept, where visible neoplasia is removed by ER followed by ablation of all the residual flat Barrett epithelium [ ]. Detection and resection of visible neoplasia are critical. Barrett’s EAC is readily missed as it is typically subtle. Truly flat HGD is rare, accounting for only 20% of cases, and is usually attributable to a missed lesion. Missed lesions can result in the inappropriate application of ablative therapies to treat undiagnosed EAC rather than dysplasia, which risks undetected disease progressing beyond the criteria for endoscopic treatment [ ]. Higher rates of endoscopic resection (ER), compared with ablation as monotherapy, are associated with lower rates of recurrent neoplasia after successful EET [ , ]. Before initiating therapy, patients must be appropriately counselled. They should understand the requirements of the EET protocol, which typically involves 4–5 treatment sessions at three-monthly intervals, followed by ongoing surveillance. Adherence to high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy is essential, as inadequate acid control has been repeatedly shown to be a critical driver for incomplete response to EET [ , ]. Advice regarding weight loss and smoking cessation should also be offered. Patients with BE are often co-morbid, with a high rate of morbidity and mortality from disease unrelated to EAC [ , ]. Surveillance following ER is a reasonable strategy in these patients [ ]. Careful patient selection, clear counselling, and incorporation of patient preferences are therefore central to decision-making around endoscopic therapy in Barrett’s. Technical Overview In the following section, we will outline the ER and ablative techniques available to the BE endoscopist, as well as the evidence and practical aspects which may influence technique selection. Endoscopic Resection ER is now the mainstay treatment for visible BE lesions having demonstrated excellent safety and efficacy, and similar overall survival when compared with surgery [ , ]. The main ER techniques are endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) and endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD). Endoscopic Mucosal Resection EMR is generally performed under conscious sedation as a day-case procedure. It is facilitated by cap or band-ligation assisted techniques. The latter, also called multiband mucosectomy (MBM), is preferred, having demonstrated superior efficiency and cost-effectiveness [ ]. It is performed using an over the scope system – a transparent cap containing 6 rubber bands, a cranking device and releasing wires. The MBM kit also includes a hexagonal braided polypectomy snare. It involves the following steps: (1) marking the abnormal area with the snare-tip, leaving a margin of normal tissue around the lesion; (2) creation of a pseudopolyp, using suction to drag the target mucosa into the cap and deploying one band; (3) placing the snare around the pseudopolyp, resting underneath the rubber band, and (4) transection of the tissue captured using a pure coagulation current ( ). This process can be repeated such that larger lesions are removed in overlapping pieces, to reduce the risk of tissue bridges. Intramucosal bleeding can usually be managed with the tip of the same snare using soft coagulation. Occasionally haemostatic forceps may be required. The cap-assisted technique requires an over-the-scope oblique transparent cap. First, the lesion is elevated with submucosal injection to separate the mucosa and submucosa from the underlying muscularis propria. A crescent-shaped snare is then pre-looped along the distal rim of the cap, and suction is applied to draw the lifted tissue into the cap. Tightening of the snare creates a pseudopolyp, which is subsequently resected using electrocautery. Pech et al. [ ] demonstrated the safety and efficacy of EMR followed by ablation in the treatment of 1,000 patients with T1a EAC. Complete remission of intestinal metaplasia (CR-IM) was achieved in 96.3%. During 5 years of follow-up, recurrence occurred in 14.5% although this was managed endoscopically in the majority (79%) such that long-term complete remission was achieved in 93.8% of patients overall. Bleeding, perforation, and stricture formation were observed in 1.4%, 0.1%, and 1.3% of cases, respectively. In a multicentre series examining the risk factors for adverse events (AE) after MBM ( N = 3,827), 35 cases (0.9% [95% confidence interval, CI, 0.6–1.3]) resulted in delayed bleeding and perforation occurred in 17 (0.4% [95% CI, 0.3–0.7]), the majority of which (88%) were managed endoscopically or conservatively [ ]. Submucosal injection did not prevent perforations. The tension at the upper and lower esophageal sphincters prevents inadvertent suction of the muscle into the cap, and if this does occur, the rubber band is not strong enough to hold it in place, rendering this technique very safe. The limitation of EMR is that the resection size is limited by the diameter of the distal cap, so larger lesions must be removed piecemeal. The lesion size cut-off for en bloc resection is typically quoted as 20 mm, although this is probably optimistic; in a meta-analysis including 24 EMR studies where the median lesion size was 15.8 mm, only 37% were removed en bloc [ ]. Furthermore, underlying fibrosis secondary to chronic inflammation may hinder suction during MBM and cap-assisted snare-capture, which may result in smaller resections or technical failure. Although submucosa is often included in the EMR specimen, the depth of the resection plane cannot be controlled by the endoscopist, which may impact completeness of resection when submucosal disease is present [ , ]. Overall, esophageal EMR, mostly performed using MBM, offers high rates of long-term remission for intramucosal disease, with low procedure-related morbidity when applied in experienced centres. Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection ESD is more resource intensive and technically challenging than EMR. It typically requires a general anaesthetic or deep sedation using propofol and occasionally necessitates hospital admission. The advantages of this technique are that it enables en bloc resection of lesions of any size or morphology, facilitates ER of fibrotic lesions, and allows the operator to control a deeper resection plane. experienced centres. Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection ESD is more resource intensive and technically challenging than EMR. It typically requires a general anaesthetic or deep sedation using propofol and occasionally necessitates hospital admission. The advantages of this technique are that it enables en bloc resection of lesions of any size or morphology, facilitates ER of fibrotic lesions, and allows the operator to control a deeper resection plane. ESD is performed using a clear distal cap and a dedicated electrosurgical microknife, typically 1.5 mm in length. The target area for resection is delineated by placing markings at least 2 mm from the visible margin to account for potential subsquamous extension. A submucosal lift is created, followed by a circumferential incision and submucosal dissection to achieve en bloc resection ( ). Intraprocedural bleeding is typically controlled using the ESD-knife or dedicated haemostatic devices as required. The choice of knife (non-insulated, insulated, scissor-type, bipolar) is at the discretion of the endoscopist. Modifications such as tunnelling, traction, and saline-immersion have emerged which improve the safety and efficiency of ESD, as well as facilitating resection of more extensive lesions [ , ]. Data on the safety and efficacy of ESD in the treatment of BE-neoplasia are limited to small, predominantly retrospective cohort studies, with limited long-term follow-up. In a meta-analysis of 11 studies ( N = 501, median lesion size 27 mm [95% CI, 20.9–33.1), Yang et al. reported pooled en bloc, R0, and curative resection rates of 92.9% (95% CI, 90.3%–95.2%), 74.5% (95% CI, 66.3%–81.9%), and 64.9% (95% CI, 55.7%–73.6%), respectively. Pooled rates of perforation and bleeding were 1.5% (95% CI, 0.4–3.0%) and 1.7% (95% CI, 0.6–3.4%), respectively, with esophageal strictures occurring in 11.6% (95% CI, 0.9–29.6%). Recurrence after curative resection was uncommon (0.17%; 95% CI, 0–0.3%) over a mean follow-up of 22.9 months (95% CI, 17.5–28.3). Overall, ESD provides high rates of en bloc and curative resection with minimal recurrence, and, when performed by experienced endoscopists, constitutes safe and definitive endoscopic treatment. Technique Selection: EMR vs. ESD Selecting the optimal ER technique for BE-neoplasia remains a challenge, as several factors must be balanced: curative (R0) resection, ER-specimen accuracy, long-term remission, safety, resource use, and local expertise. Wide variation in recommendations among published guidelines reflects this challenge [ , – ]. There is one published randomised controlled trial (RCT) investigating EMR ( N = 20) vs ESD ( N = 20) in the treatment of BE-neoplasia, which was powered to determine comparative efficacy, i.e., single session R0 resection [ ]. ESD achieved significantly higher rates of en bloc resection (100% vs. 15%, with ESD vs. EMR, respectively, p < 0.001), at the expense of longer procedure duration and greater requirement for general anaesthetic. EMR and ESD achieved similar rates of complete remission from BE-neoplasia (CRN), and on this basis, the authors concluded that ESD has no advantage over EMR. However, the follow-up duration was short, the lesions were small (mean maximum diameter 14 mm and 16 mm in EMR and ESD groups, respectively), and the final histology was predominantly (30/40, 75%) intramucosal disease. There have been 3 meta-analyses published recently, evaluating the outcomes of EMR vs. ESD, which unsurprisingly all reported significantly higher pooled en bloc and R0 resection rates with ESD [ , , ]. Radadiya et al. and Fujiyoshi et al. observed similar rates of curative resection, eradication of BE and overall safety profile. However, Gallegos et al. [ ] reported an increased risk of AE with ESD (risk difference for bleeding, stricture, and perforation: 0.01, p = 0.005; 0.01, p = 0 0.01; and 0.04, p = 0.04, respectively). Fujiyoshi et al. demonstrated a trend towards lower recurrence following ESD (odds ratio [OR] 0.35, p = 0.058), and Gallegos et al. demonstrated that when RFA was not performed, recurrence was lower in the ESD group (OR 0.22, p = 0.04). It is important to note that the comparative data included in these meta-analyses are influenced by selection bias from lesion-based technique algorithms and marked heterogeneity in definitions of treatment success, remission and recurrence. In a single-centre retrospective analysis of 157 patients with HGD or EAC (87 EMR, 70 ESD), recurrence after confirmed CRN was markedly lower with ESD than EMR (1.9% vs. 13%, p < 0.05). The 3-year cumulative incidence of neoplastic recurrence was 4.2% after ESD and 18.3% after EMR, despite adjunctive RFA use in both groups [ ]. From a practical perspective, certain lesion characteristics immediately lend themselves to ESD; i.e., fibrotic or bulky (Paris 0-Is) lesions which cannot be suctioned into the MBM cap. In fact, most guidelines recommend ESD in this context [ , , ]. Otherwise, technique selection is based upon the pre-resection endoscopic prediction of the underlying histopathology, with EMR employed for ostensibly intramucosal disease while ESD is favoured when submucosal invasion is suspected [ ]. From a practical perspective, certain lesion characteristics immediately lend themselves to ESD; i.e., fibrotic or bulky (Paris 0-Is) lesions which cannot be suctioned into the MBM cap. In fact, most guidelines recommend ESD in this context [ , , ]. Otherwise, technique selection is based upon the pre-resection endoscopic prediction of the underlying histopathology, with EMR employed for ostensibly intramucosal disease while ESD is favoured when submucosal invasion is suspected [ ]. Other imaging tools such as EUS are unable to reliably determine invasion depth [ ]. Technique selection therefore hinges upon optical assessment; however, endoscopic lesion assessment is inaccurate, even amongst experts. While expert interventional endoscopists can reliably distinguish dysplasia from EAC and T1 from T2 disease, in a study of 19 experts reviewing still images (using high-definition endoscopes and VCE), pooled sensitivity for differentiating T1a from T1b was only 43.8% [ ]. The value of en bloc resection extends beyond margin status: ER is a critical staging and risk-stratification tool. Post-resection management hinges on histology to estimate the lymph node metastasis (LNM) risk and guide subsequent therapy, therefore, an intact specimen is essential. In a retrospective study of 76 ER specimens (36 EMR, 40 ESD), Krause et al. [ ] found that one-third contained no submucosa, with no difference between EMR and ESD. Although this could imply comparable specimen quality with both techniques, the substantial inter-centre variability seen only in ESD highlights the impact of operator technique. It stands to reason that piecemeal EMR may risk missing important adverse features (e.g., foci of lymphovascular invasion [LVI] or poor differentiation). By contrast, in the ESD specimen, preserved tissue layers enable differentiation between T1a and T1b EAC, while inclusion of superficial muscularis propria further enhances assessment of invasion depth and the integrity of the deep margin [ ]. In the absence of large, well-designed RCTs, no definitive recommendation on technique selection can be made. Nonetheless, based on existing evidence and our clinical experience, we suggest the following principles may guide practice. Visible BE dysplasia of any size is readily managed with MBM-EMR. When T1a/b EAC is suspected, an en bloc resection method warrants consideration to avoid undertreatment resulting from understaging at endoscopic assessment. When local expertise allows, ESD should be considered for lesions >15 mm, particularly when Paris 0-IIc morphology or a disrupted surface pattern is present. Two ongoing RCTs ( NCT05276791 , NCT03427346 ) should provide further clarity in this evolving area. The importance of MDT discussion and shared decision-making with patients, bearing mind their overall health and individual values, cannot be overstated. Ablation BE-neoplasia arises in a field of metaplastic change; therefore, ablation is generally recommended after successful ER to minimise recurrent or metachronous neoplasia [ , ]. In the landmark multicentre European trial, EURO-II, Phoa et al. [ ] demonstrated that amongst 132 patients referred for ER for BE-neoplasia followed by ablative therapy, CR-IM was achieved in 87% of patients by intention-to-treat and 93% per protocol, with low neoplasic recurrence (4%) and a favourable safety profile. A multicentre RCT comparing stepwise ER to ablation for the treatment of BE ≤5 cm with HGD/EAC, clinical efficacy was similar in the two groups but more AE were observed with stepwise ER [ ]; therefore, this practice is not recommended. Ablation is applied as monotherapy for patients with flat HGD (i.e., no visible lesion detected after expert assessment), as well as patients with LGD confirmed on two separate endoscopies by expert pathologists, as in both scenarios ablation reduces the risk of progression to EAC compared with endoscopic surveillance [ , , ]. The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recently concluded that RFA for confirmed LGD is cost-effective compared with surveillance at a willingness-to-pay threshold of GBP 20,000 (EUR 22,700) per QALY. For HGD and T1a EAC, they found that EMR plus RFA is cost-effective versus surveillance, and that both RFA followed by surveillance and RFA alone are cheaper and more effective than esophagectomy [ ]. Adherence to high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy is crucial in promoting healing and in overall treatment success, as is adherence to 3-monthly treatment intervals [ ]. In selected individuals with limited life expectancy, a more tailored approach may be appropriate. In a retrospective analysis of the Dutch BE registry, among 94 patients who underwent ER for BE-neoplasia without subsequent ablation, due to clinical reasons or comorbidity, only 18% developed recurrent neoplasia after a median of 18 months, all of which were managed endoscopically. Of the comorbid patients, 40% died from unrelated causes with no EAC-related mortality [ ]. In patients with significant comorbidity, surveillance should be considered over multiple sessions of ablation, particularly if

In a retrospective analysis of the Dutch BE registry, among 94 patients who underwent ER for BE-neoplasia without subsequent ablation, due to clinical reasons or comorbidity, only 18% developed recurrent neoplasia after a median of 18 months, all of which were managed endoscopically. Of the comorbid patients, 40% died from unrelated causes with no EAC-related mortality [ ]. In patients with significant comorbidity, surveillance should be considered over multiple sessions of ablation, particularly if factors predicting poor response (large hiatus hernia, long BE segment, baggy esophagus) are present. Radiofrequency Ablation RFA applies controlled thermal energy to the Barrett’s mucosa, producing superficial necrosis that clears metaplastic and dysplastic tissue and allows squamous re-epithelialisation. It is by far the most robustly studied ablation technique. Its safety, effectiveness at eradicating BE and durability at maintaining remission has been repeatedly demonstrated in RCT and real-world settings across Europe and the USA [ , , , ]. The Dutch reported the outcomes of 1,386 patients treated with RFA, as monotherapy (38%) or followed by ER (62%), over a 10-year period [ ]. The overall stricture rate was 15%, although the majority were mild and managed with a median of 2 endoscopic dilatation sessions. Bleeding occurred at a rate of 2% per procedure, and there were no perforations related to RFA. CE-BE was achieved in 94% of cases, with 3% neoplastic recurrence during a median follow-up period of 43 months. After remission was achieved, the annual incidence of LGD/HGD/EAC was 1% and 0.8% for HGD/EAC which is comparable to non-dysplastic BE [ ]. These results are superior to those reported in other real-world registries, where lower rates of treatment success and higher rates of recurrence were observed [ , ]. Aside from relatively higher rates of ER for HGD/EAC in the Dutch cohort, following a stringent RFA protocol may account for this difference. RFA is conducted by performing stepwise circumferential and focal ablative therapy using dedicated ablation catheters (Barrx system, Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA) [ , ]. Firstly, circumferential ablation is performed using the Halo 360 Express catheter, a 4 cm self-sizing balloon introduced over a guidewire. Under direct endoscopic vision, the balloon is inflated and therapy delivered using a foot pedal. The process is repeated for longer segments, allowing small overlap between ablation zones, until all the visible BE is ablated. Two ablations are performed to each area, using 10 J/cm 2 of energy, cleaning the catheter and the mucosa (using a clear distal cap) in between ablations to prevent stricture formation [ ]. At subsequent treatments, a focal device is used, available in 3 different sizes (Barrx™ ultra long, Barrx™ 90 and Barrx™ 60 focal catheters), placed over-the-scope in the 12 o’clock position. The tip of the scope is deflected upwards to bring the electrode in close contact with the mucosa while energy is being delivered; 3 ablations at 12 J/cm 2 , without interval cleaning [ ]. It is imperative that circumferential treatment of the gastro-esophageal junction (GEJ) is performed again at the second session, as this is the site of most (∼75%) recurrences [ , , ]. A smaller through-the-scope RFA catheter can be used to treat residual islands at follow-up sessions ( ). Argon Plasma Coagulation, Hybrid APC, and Cryotherapy Alternative ablation techniques include argon plasma coagulation (APC), hybrid APC, and cryoballoon ablation (CBA). APC is a non-contact ablation technique; energy is transmitted via ionised argon gas. It is delivered in a distal-to-proximal stroking motion starting at the GEJ, using a forward-firing APC catheter projected 1 cm beyond the scope tip on forced coagulation at 60 W. In the only RCT comparing RFA to APC following ER for HGD/EAC ( N = 116), clinical efficacy and safety were similar, while APC was associated with lower cost. It is worth noting that there were only a small number of patients with very long segment BE (>10 cm), more drop-outs in the APC group and the rate of CE-BE with RFA was far lower than that recorded in previously published data, at 55% [ ]. In their 2024 guidance, NICE noted that in very long segments, RFA may be more efficient than APC because each APC application covers a much smaller area [ ]. Hybrid APC was designed to reduce the risk of AE, by first injecting saline into the submucosal space, creating a cushion that protects the deeper layers from thermal damage. Ablation and submucosal injection are delivered via the same probe (hybrid APC probe, Erbe, Tübingen, Germany). Hybrid APC was designed to reduce the risk of AE, by first injecting saline into the submucosal space, creating a cushion that protects the deeper layers from thermal damage. Ablation and submucosal injection are delivered via the same probe (hybrid APC probe, Erbe, Tübingen, Germany). In a prospective multicentre European trial ( N = 154), CR-IM was achieved in 98%, with sustained remission of dysplasia in only 71% after 2 years of follow-up [ ]. Knabe et al. reported similar rates of BE eradication with hybrid APC (82.9%) and RFA (74.2%) following ER in a randomised setting ( N = 110), with a significantly higher stricture rate observed following RFA (14.9% vs. 3.7%, p = 0.05). Unfortunately, this trial was impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic, with only 26% of patients completing the full study protocol. In a US pilot study, the stricture rate with hybrid APC was 9%, similar to previous reports following RFA [ , ]. Long-term follow-up data are, however, lacking. Furthermore, success of both APC and hybrid APC is very operator dependent. CBA is delivered using a compliant 3 cm balloon cooled to −80 to −85°C by nitrous oxide released from a handheld controller (CbFAS, C2 Cryoballoon, Pentax Medical Corporation). The standard 8-s dose creates a 2 cm ice patch, delivered via a foot pedal. The catheter is passed through a therapeutic scope, the balloon inflated in the stomach and then positioned at the GEJ for focal applications. Cryotherapy was hypothesised to potentially reach deeper tissue than RFA while preserving the extracellular matrix, without an associated increase in stricture risk. Published data from small prospective series report CR-IM rates between 72 and 88%, durable remission from dysplasia (2% recurrence rate at 3.9 years) and a similar safety profile to other ablative therapies (stricture rate 9.7–15%) [ – ]. More recently, a large ( N = 107) multicentre prospective trial investigating CBA in the treatment of neoplastic BE up to 5 cm, with or without prior ER, CE-BE was achieved in 94% (95% CI, 90%–98%) with no neoplastic recurrence following remission, and a stricture rate of 12% (95% CI, 7%–19%) [ ]. There are no RCTS comparing RFA and CBA as yet. Taking all this data together, RFA remains first-line therapy for BE-neoplasia having demonstrated excellent safety, efficacy and durability on long-term follow-up in large cohorts in a number of different settings, although clearly the best results are achieved in centres of excellence. Although Hybrid APC and CBA may be promising new techniques, robust, well-powered studies and longer follow-up are required before we can determine an algorithm for selecting between these techniques. Management after Endoscopic Therapy Immediate Post ER and Ablation Care Patients are usually advised to maintain a liquid diet for 24 h after ER or ablation, gradually building up their diet to more solid food over a few days. High-dose twice daily proton pump inhibitor therapy is required to promote healing. Regardless of the ER method, the risk of stricture formation increases with the extent of the luminal circumference which was resected [ ]. Although an optimal strategy for post-ER stricture prevention has not been demonstrated, corticosteroids (oral or intralesional) are generally recommended following an ER-defect involving >50% of the circumference [ ]. Before discharge, patients should receive clear safety-netting information, including defined routes to contact the endoscopy unit should any complications occur. Specimen Handling and Treatment Options after ER Management following ER is entirely dependent upon the information obtained from the ER specimen. Therefore, careful handling and assessment of the ER specimen is crucial. It must be pinned to a corkboard or paraffin to optimise orientation and assessment of the margins. There is a high degree of interobserver variability in reporting on submucosal invasion depth and LVI, crucial histopathologic parameters, highlighting the importance of expert pathologist review, ideally by two pathologists, to ensure accurate risk stratification [ ]. Currently, ER is considered definitive therapy of T1a and superficial (<500 μm) T1b EAC in the absence of additional factors such as poor differentiation or LVI, provided clear resection margins were achieved [ , ]. This approach reflects the low LNM rates (2–4%) seen in high-quality retrospective series when these criteria are met, weighed against the significant morbidity and mortality associated with esophagectomy [ , , ]. The presence of deeper submucosal invasion, LVI or poor differentiation has traditionally been linked with higher rates of LNM, approaching 60%, and therefore esophagectomy and/or adjuvant chemoradiotherapy is recommended provided patient factors do not preclude treatment [ , , ]. However, historic data from surgical specimens may have understaged T1 EAC and overestimated LNM risk as a result. More recent analyses of ER

were achieved [ , ]. This approach reflects the low LNM rates (2–4%) seen in high-quality retrospective series when these criteria are met, weighed against the significant morbidity and mortality associated with esophagectomy [ , , ]. The presence of deeper submucosal invasion, LVI or poor differentiation has traditionally been linked with higher rates of LNM, approaching 60%, and therefore esophagectomy and/or adjuvant chemoradiotherapy is recommended provided patient factors do not preclude treatment [ , , ]. However, historic data from surgical specimens may have understaged T1 EAC and overestimated LNM risk as a result. More recent analyses of ER specimens, which are processed using thinner slices, report LNM rates between 9 and 20% for high-risk T1a EAC, and 8–11% for high-risk T1b EAC [ , , ]. These data are derived from small, retrospective series. The ongoing PREFER study ( NCT03222635 ), is a prospective series investigating the outcomes of close surveillance for patients with high-risk T1a/T1b EAC. In the event of a non-curative resection, staging EUS and CT-PET should be performed around 6 weeks following ER (to avoid local inflammation confounding image interpretation), followed by MDT discussion. A watchful approach is increasingly being recognised as a reasonable alternative to esophagectomy. As the criteria for ER are set to expand, deep margin involvement may become a more frequent challenge for the MDT. In a retrospective analysis of 101 ER specimens with apparent tumour positive deep margins, only 75% were confirmed R1 after second expert pathologist assessment. Of those, 50% had no residual neoplasia. All residual neoplasia was endoscopically visible and mostly amenable to endoscopic curative therapy [ ]. Therefore, endoscopic reassessment may be preferable to immediate referral for non-endoscopic therapy, although again the suitability of this approach requires prospective study (PREFERENCE, NL009247). Surveillance after Endoscopic Eradication Therapy Following ER, if no additional non-endoscopic therapy is required, ablation is performed until CE-BE is achieved. This can be confirmed endoscopically by the presence of a neo Z-line within 1 cm of the proximal limit of the gastric folds. Biopsies of the neosquamous epithelium and cardia are no longer performed in expert centres, as they do not influence the detection of neoplastic recurrence [ ]. Once EET is completed, ongoing surveillance is required due to the risk of recurrent or metachronous disease (1–2%) [ , , ]. This usually occurs in the first 2 years following EET, therefore in this period surveillance should be conducted in an expert BE centre [ ]. Ongoing acid suppression is crucial, although the dose can be titrated to the patient’s symptoms and endoscopic appearances. Before embarking on intensive and long-term surveillance, it is important to again consider the overall benefit to the individual patient. In a cohort of 1,154 patients who completed EET, during a follow-up period of 59 months, the risk of unrelated mortality was 40 times higher than the risk of death from recurrent EAC. Furthermore, the risk of unrelated death could be reliably predicted using the Charlson Comorbidity Index (C-statistic 0.78) [ ]. Conclusion EET has transformed the management of BE-neoplasia, offering high rates of cure and durable remission, without incurring unnecessary risk. Treatment is nuanced, with best outcomes achieved where expertise is concentrated. High-quality optical assessment and ER of visible BE-neoplasia are required before embarking on ablative therapy. Careful patient selection, counselling and MDT discussion are crucial particularly given the competing risks of comorbidity in this population. Importantly, ongoing prospective studies are set to refine technique selection and post-resection management, helping us tailor therapy more precisely to lesion behaviour and patient factors.
